Kevin Roose is obsessed with the moments in history when “the fabric of the world changes or goes in a new direction.” The race to build artificial general intelligence (AGI)—a world-saving or world-ending technology, depending on who you ask—is one of those moments. Roose has spent the past decade reporting on that race, with access to the people and decisions shaping it at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind.

For his new book, The AGI Chronicles, Roose interviewed 150 people to uncover a history largely hidden within AI labs and guarded by nondisclosure agreements. The book goes inside the labs where researchers train and test AI models, including what went on behind the scenes of Sam Altman’s dramatic firing https://every.?ev_audience=free and https://every.?ev_audience=free reinstatement https://every.?ev_audience=free at OpenAI.

In his second appearance https://every.?ev_audience=free on The Every Podcast https://every.?ev_audience=free, Roose joins Natalia Quintero https://every.?ev_audience=free to discuss his role in making sense of Silicon Valley for the wider world and the questions that guided his book: “Are we careening toward an existential cliff? Is it all hype?” His reporting left him convinced that while the risks are real, the outcome isn’t predetermined. “I don’t think anything is set in stone or predestined,” he says. “The choices we make right now matter a lot in terms of how the next few years or few decades go.”

Watch on X https://every.?ev_audience=free or YouTube https://every.?ev_audience=free or listen on Spotify https://every.?ev_audience=free or Apple Podcasts https://every._?ev_audience=free. You can also read the transcript https://every.?ev_audience=free.

Here are the highlights:

 * The moment Roose “felt” the AGI. At OpenAI, Ilya Sutskever was known for walking desk to desk telling colleagues, “You must feel the AGI,” a phrase Roose borrows in The AGI Chronicles. Roose first felt it during his encounter with Sydney https://every.?ev_audience=free, “the deranged alter ego of Microsoft’s Bing chat function.” It wasn’t sentient or conscious, but the technology underneath it was powerful enough to make him want to understand how AI systems are built and what drives the companies racing to release them—sometimes cutting corners to beat their rivals.
 * He had a “council of Claudes” review his work. Roose wrote all 450 pages of the book in a year with “this brain and these fingers,” supported by human editors and a researcher. He used AI to organize his research in NotebookLM and review his chapters using a “council” of Claude agents https://every.?ev_audience=free, which included an AI skeptic, an AI historian, and a “Walter Isaacson–style craftsperson” who judged whether the story was a joy to read. A master editor agent combined their feedback into a single document. The council caught a couple of factual errors his human editors had missed—a sign, Roose says, of how much the tools have improved.
 * He sees his role as “demystifying” AI for the public. Roose has always loved exploring technology, from building web pages as a kid to tinkering with new AI tools today. His role as a tech journalist is also to explain these technologies. He recently left the New York Times to start a media company with Casey Newton, his longtime Hard Fork co-host. Their new show, Machine Gods, produced in partnership with NPR, aims to make AI “fun and accessible”. “The most important thing I could be doing at this moment,” he says, “is helping people understand what’s going on in San Francisco at these AI companies, with AI in general, and what it means for their lives and how they should prepare and adapt.”

Listen for an inside account of the people and decisions that shaped modern AI—and the choices still to come.
